models.name: Bolex Stereo
models.summary: A 3-D attachment for the non-reflex H-series, recording both eyes on one strip of ordinary 16mm film. Twin rear lenses sit 5.3 mm apart and a prism block widens that to an interocular of 64 mm, close to the average human spacing. f/2.8, no focusing: it is set at the hyperfocal distance for about 10 ft and left there. The matching 20 mm projection lens carries polarising filters at 135 and 45 degrees, so showing the results needs polarised glasses and a silver screen. Paillard's own fitting instructions name the 16mm De Luxe with its Octameter finder as the camera the system is built around, and the fitting is real work: the turret centre post comes out and is replaced with one of two supplied lengths depending on whether the turret has a lever, and the Octameter is moved forward onto a standoff bracket. That last part has a consequence Paillard spells out: with the finder pushed forward its parallax markings no longer read true, so the standoff carries its own conversion scale. Film 30ft away and you set the finder to 15. Projection uses twin lenses with the polarisers crossed in each light channel, and Paillard claimed they fitted 90 per cent of modern projectors, with a Type G version for its own. US$397.50 in 1952, which was more than most of the cameras it bolted onto.

sources.title: Hess, Hillary (2024). "Bolex Stereo", in James Layton (ed.), Film Atlas

sources.title: Bolex Stereo, Paillard fitting and projection instructions
sources.note: Paillard's own sheet, and the source of the fitting, the standoff parallax scale, the f/2.8 to f/22 diaphragm and the projection arrangement. It agrees with the Film Atlas entry where the two overlap: crossed polarisers in each channel, and the same aperture. Scanned by Pacific Rim Camera.

sources.title: Fits the non-reflex Bolex only
sources.note: The reflex prism of an H-16 Rex occupies the space the attachment's own optics need. Anyone matching one to a camera should check which they have before buying.

sources.title: Still wanted
sources.note: A Paillard instruction sheet has since been read and is cited above, which covers fitting and projection. Pacific Rim also lists a "Bolex Sterero Instruction Book" (their spelling); whether that is the same document under another name is not settled. The end of production is also unsettled: about 1954 is the Film Atlas reading, and how many were sold at that price is not recorded anywhere found so far.
